lead: The third law fixes the zero of entropy. At absolute zero, a perfect crystal at equilibrium has zero entropy, so entropy can be listed as an absolute value and not only as a change. It also explains why 0 K is a limit, not a target you can hit. Cryogenics, low-temperature physics and the absolute entropies in chemical data tables all rest on it. Steam tables, met later with pure substances, instead take an arbitrary zero at the triple point of water, which is enough because engineering problems need only changes of entropy.
prereq: You need: entropy as a property and the molecular view of entropy, S = k ln W.

sections.h3: Nernst theorem and the third law

blocks.text: Cool a substance and its entropy falls. Early measurements could give only ΔS between two temperatures. Nernst asked what happens as T → 0 K. His heat theorem says that for a condensed system at equilibrium, the entropy change of any isothermal process tends to zero as T tends to zero. In symbols, ΔS → 0 as T → 0 K.

From this, Planck proposed a fixed zero: for a perfect crystal at 0 K, S = 0. This is the third law. A perfect crystal has every atom on its proper lattice site, with no mixing and no frozen disorder. There is only one way to arrange it, so the statistical entropy S = k<sub>B</sub> ln W gives S = k<sub>B</sub> ln 1 = 0. Here k<sub>B</sub> is Boltzmann's constant (1.381 × 10<sup>−23</sup> J/K) and W is the number of equally likely arrangements.

The law does not say that every real material has zero entropy at 0 K. It says a perfect crystal at equilibrium does. A glass or a crystal with trapped defects does not. That leftover is residual entropy.
With a zero at 0 K, entropy at any T is an absolute value. Heat the sample reversibly from 0 K; at each step dS = δQ<sub>rev</sub>/T = c<sub>p</sub> dT/T. Integrate:

blocks.where: S(T) is absolute entropy at temperature T in J/(mol·K); c<sub>p</sub> is heat capacity at constant pressure in J/(mol·K); T is absolute temperature in K. This holds when no phase change happens on the way up; if the solid melts, boils or changes crystal form at T<sub>tr</sub>, add ΔH<sub>tr</sub>/T<sub>tr</sub> for each change, where ΔH<sub>tr</sub> is the heat of that change in J/mol.

blocks.text: Near 0 K the heat capacity is too small to measure over the last part. Debye's model gives c<sub>p</sub> = aT<sup>3</sup>, where a is a constant for the material with units J/(mol·K<sup>4</sup>). Put this into the integral from 0 to a low measured temperature T<sub>1</sub>:

blocks.where: a is the Debye constant in J/(mol·K<sup>4</sup>); T<sub>1</sub> is the lowest measured temperature in K; the result is in J/(mol·K).

blocks.text: Above T<sub>1</sub> you add the measured ∫(c<sub>p</sub>/T)dT pieces. If c<sub>p</sub> were constant, S = c<sub>p</sub> ln T + constant. As T → 0, ln T → −∞, so S would run to minus infinity. That cannot match S = 0. Real c<sub>p</sub> falls to zero as T → 0 (as aT³ in an insulator, roughly in proportion to T in a metal), so c<sub>p</sub>/T stays finite and the integral converges. The third law therefore forces c<sub>p</sub> → 0 as T → 0 K. Most exam questions ask for the statement and the unattainability argument; numerical absolute entropies appear only occasionally.

Cooling by adiabatic demagnetisation uses a magnetic salt. Magnetise it isothermally, releasing heat. Then isolate it and remove the field adiabatically. The spins disarrange and the sample cools. Repeat with a new starting temperature. Each step lowers T, but the entropy curves for different field strengths approach each other near 0 K. The temperature drop per step shrinks.

Unattainability statement: no finite sequence of processes can bring a system to exactly 0 K. You can approach it, never arrive. This is equivalent to the third law for equilibrium systems. The unattainability form is often easier to apply than the Nernst form. It forbids a machine that reaches 0 K in finite steps. It does not forbid getting very close: laboratories reach microkelvin or nanokelvin. The last fraction of a kelvin is paid for with many steps.

The reason is the Nernst theorem itself: as T → 0, the entropy change of the isothermal magnetising step shrinks towards zero, so the entropy gap that each adiabatic demagnetisation can use, and with it the temperature drop per step, shrinks too. Together with c<sub>p</sub> → 0, that is the thermodynamic signature of the third law.

figure.caption: The worked example’s solid, with c = 0.002T³ J/(mol·K): its entropy rises from zero to 0.667 J/(mol·K) at 10 K. If c stayed at its 10 K value of 2 J/(mol·K), the dashed curve would fall below zero and without limit as T falls, which the third law forbids.

spec.aria: Entropy against temperature from 0 to 10 K. A solid curve S equals a T cubed over 3 starts at zero and reaches 0.667 J/(mol K) at 10 K. A dashed curve for constant heat capacity, 0.667 plus 2 ln(T/10), drops below minus 3 near 1 K.

examples.question: A non-metallic solid follows the Debye law below 10 K, with c<sub>p</sub> = aT<sup>3</sup>, where a = 0.002 J/(mol·K<sup>4</sup>). Take S = 0 at 0 K. Find the absolute entropy at 10 K.
steps: Write the heat capacity: c<sub>p</sub> = 0.002 T<sup>3</sup> J/(mol·K), with T in K.
For reversible heating at constant pressure: dS = c<sub>p</sub> dT/T = (aT<sup>3</sup>/T) dT = aT<sup>2</sup> dT.
Integrate from 0 K to 10 K: S = ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>10</sup> aT<sup>2</sup> dT = a[T<sup>3</sup>/3]<sub>0</sub><sup>10</sup>.
Put in a = 0.002 J/(mol·K<sup>4</sup>) and T = 10 K: S = 0.002 × 10<sup>3</sup>/3 J/(mol·K).
examples.answer: The absolute entropy at 10 K is 0.667 J/(mol·K).
examples.check:
a = 0.002
T = 10.0
S = a * T**3 / 3
print(round(S, 3))

traps: S = 0 at 0 K is for a perfect crystal at equilibrium. Glasses, solid solutions and crystals with frozen-in defects keep residual entropy, so do not apply zero blindly.
Absolute zero is unattainable, not just difficult. A finite number of adiabatic demagnetisation steps never reaches exactly 0 K; microkelvin is not zero.
Do not integrate S = c<sub>p</sub> ln T down to 0 K. Use c<sub>p</sub> = aT<sup>3</sup> and the integral aT<sup>3</sup>/3 over the low-temperature range.
c<sub>p</sub> and c<sub>v</sub> tend to zero as T → 0 K. Treating them as constant near absolute zero gives a divergent, negative entropy.
Entropy change between two states needs no third law. Absolute entropy, as in tables, does need the third-law zero.

quiz.q: State the third law of thermodynamics for a perfect crystal.
quiz.a: For a perfect crystal at equilibrium, S → 0 as T → 0 K.

quiz.q: What does the Nernst heat theorem say?
quiz.a: For a condensed system at equilibrium, ΔS → 0 as T → 0 K for an isothermal process.

quiz.q: Why does the classical expression S = c<sub>p</sub> ln T fail near absolute zero?
quiz.a: If c<sub>p</sub> is constant, S = c<sub>p</sub> ln T + constant. As T → 0, ln T → −∞, so S → −∞, which contradicts S = 0. Real c<sub>p</sub> → 0 as T → 0, so c<sub>p</sub>/T stays finite and the integral converges.

quiz.q: Why can a finite number of adiabatic demagnetisation steps not reach 0 K?
quiz.a: Each step removes the field adiabatically, but the entropy curves for different fields merge near 0 K. The temperature drop per step shrinks, so finite steps approach 0 K but never reach it.

quiz.q: A solid has c<sub>p</sub> = aT<sup>3</sup> with a = 0.003 J/(mol·K<sup>4</sup>) below 5 K. Taking S = 0 at 0 K, find S at 5 K.
quiz.a: S = ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>5</sup> (aT<sup>3</sup>/T) dT = ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>5</sup> aT<sup>2</sup> dT = aT<sup>3</sup>/3 = 0.003 × 125/3 = 0.125 J/(mol·K).

quiz.q: A glass is cooled to 0 K. Does the third law force its entropy to zero? Explain.
quiz.a: No. A glass is not a perfect crystal at equilibrium. Its frozen disorder gives residual entropy at 0 K, so S(0) > 0. The third law sets zero only for a perfect crystal at equilibrium.

quiz.q: Show why the third law implies c<sub>p</sub> → 0 as T → 0 K.
quiz.a: S(0) is finite. For heating from 0 K, S(T) − S(0) = ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>T</sup> (c<sub>p</sub>/T) dT must converge. If c<sub>p</sub> tended to a nonzero constant, the integral would diverge as ln T. Therefore c<sub>p</sub> must tend to zero; the Debye form c<sub>p</sub> = aT<sup>3</sup> is one model that does this.

beyond: Not for the exam. Absolute entropy is tabulated for refrigerants and cryogenic fluids, and the third law underpins low-temperature thermometry and adiabatic demagnetisation refrigerators. In materials science, residual entropy reveals frozen disorder in glasses and spin ice. In quantum computing, cooling to millikelvin is routine but exact 0 K remains a limit. Search for Nernst heat theorem, Debye T cubed law and residual entropy of glasses to go further.
